issues.description: The paper states 154 suffixes were identified, then says 64 were excluded for occurring in fewer than 20 words, yet claims 95 remain. 154 − 64 = 90, not 95. This five-suffix discrepancy is unaccounted for and calls into question the accuracy of the reported means for the restricted sample.
issues.quote: we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993). For the remaining 95 suffixes, the mean diagnosticity and specificity values were virtually unchanged

issues.description: A z-value of 0.60 cannot produce p < 0.01 under any standard normal distribution (it corresponds to p ≈ 0.55). Either the test statistic or the p-value is wrong. This finding supports the key claim that the congruency × specificity interaction holds for token-based measures, so the error directly affects a major result.
issues.quote: the interaction between specificity and condition was significant, such that the target spelling became used more often in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition as its specificity increased (B = 1.9, z = 2.8, p < 0.01; for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01)

issues.description: Two separate contradictions exist between the Results narrative and Table 5. For go-past time, the text reports B = 41, t = 3.837, but Table 5 shows B = 43, t = 3.76. For regressions-out, the text reports B = 0.3, z = 3.12, but Table 5 shows B = 0.25, z = 2.65. These discrepancies suggest different model runs were reported in different places, undermining confidence in which values are correct.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001) ... The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction ... (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01)

issues.description: The authors test whether the regression slope (0.9) differs significantly from 1 using F(1) = 7.44. However, the expected t-statistic for this contrast is t = (0.9 − 1)/SE = (−0.1)/0.04 = −2.5, yielding F = t² = 6.25, not 7.44. The reported F-value is inconsistent with the reported slope and standard error by approximately 19%, suggesting a calculation or reporting error in this entropy comparison.
issues.quote: We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 (SE = 0.04, t = 25.32, p < 0.0001), and that this slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01).

issues.description: Diagnosticity is verbally defined as 'the strength with which a suffix spelling predicts lexical category,' which maps onto P(category | suffix). However, the formula divides 'the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category' by 'the total number of words falling into this category'—suggesting the denominator is all words in the category (e.g., all nouns in CELEX), not all words containing the suffix. Verification against Appendix A confirms the denominator must actually be 'total words containing the suffix': for +ness, type frequency = 1242 and diagnosticity_N ≈ 0.999, consistent only if 1241/1242 is computed. The verbal description is therefore incorrect and would confuse replication attempts.
issues.quote: type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.

issues.description: The GLMM for Experiment 1 includes only a random intercept for subjects (1|subject), omitting a random intercept for items (nonwords or suffixes). In psycholinguistic experiments this is the 'language-as-fixed-effect' fallacy (Clark, 1973). Each suffix appears only twice per participant across 20 suffixes, meaning item variance is entirely absorbed into residual error, inflating the effective degrees of freedom and the risk of Type I error. All key inferences about suffix-level diagnosticity effects rest on this model.
issues.quote: This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.description: Experiment 3 tests six eye-movement measures (skips, first fixation duration, first run dwell time, go-past time, regressions-in, regressions-out) without any correction for multiple comparisons and without pre-registration. The authors explicitly state they had no a priori predictions about which measures would be affected. Finding two significant results from six tests (go-past time and regressions-out) is consistent with chance-level Type I error at α = 0.05 (expected ≈ 0.3 false positives per comparison family). This admission of exploratory intent undermines the confirmatory framing of the results.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.description: The number of words preceding the target nonword is significantly different across congruent and incongruent conditions (4.75 vs. 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05). This pre-target region establishes the syntactic context that drives the congruency manipulation; longer pre-target regions provide more contextual constraint. This unmatched variable could systematically confound the congruency effect, particularly for late measures such as go-past time and regressions-out that reflect integration processes.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.description: Comprehension accuracy is reported as '0.86%' with a range of '0.66% to 0.98%'. These values are clearly proportions (not percentages)—a true percentage of 0.86% would indicate that participants answered correctly less than 1 in 100 comprehension questions, which is implausibly poor performance. The '%' symbol is incorrectly applied throughout this sentence, constituting a reporting error for a key measure of task engagement.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.description: None of the three experiments were pre-registered. This is particularly problematic for Experiment 3, where the authors explicitly acknowledge having no specific predictions about which of six eye-movement measures would be sensitive to the manipulation, yet report a confirmatory pattern. The computational analysis involves multiple researcher choices (cutoff of 20 words, focus on three lexical categories, exclusion rules for stems) that are not pre-specified. Without pre-registration it is impossible to distinguish confirmatory from exploratory analyses.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation

issues.description: The paper states 'Our analyses consider three major lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs,' yet Appendix A includes high-frequency adverb-forming suffixes such as +LY (type frequency = 2717, the single most frequent suffix in the sample) and +ALLY (type frequency = 397), both of which show diagnosticity near zero for all three included categories. Including these suffixes without accounting for their primary function as adverb markers artificially deflates mean diagnosticity values and distorts the claim that 'the majority of written English derivational suffixes are diagnostic and specific for some lexical category.' At minimum this exclusion should be justified and its effect on the reported means quantified.
issues.quote: Our analyses consider three major lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs. Only the most frequent pronunciation was considered for each suffix.

issues.description: The General Discussion concludes that 'the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so.' However, Experiment 1 is a fully explicit metalinguistic classification task in which participants are instructed to judge whether a letter string 'looks like a noun or an adjective.' This task directly invites strategic use of explicit spelling knowledge and cannot demonstrate implicit learning. Drawing conclusions about implicit learning and automatized reading from an explicitly framed task represents an unwarranted inferential leap.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so (see our spelling and eye tracking data) suggesting that these cues facilitate access to meaning.

issues.description: The paper's central interpretive claim—that 'English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information'—is a strong functional/teleological claim about evolutionary pressure that is not testable with the reported data. The synchronic corpus statistics and behavioral experiments cannot establish that inconsistency evolved to serve meaning transmission; this requires diachronic modeling of selection pressures, which is not undertaken here. The diachronic evidence cited from Berg and Aronoff (2017) shows correlation over time but does not identify a mechanism or rule out drift.
issues.quote: English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information in the service of skilled reading.

issues.description: No standardized effect sizes (e.g., odds ratios, Cohen's d, partial η², or variance explained) are reported for any of the three experiments. Only raw regression coefficients (B) and z/t statistics are given. Without effect sizes, readers cannot evaluate practical or theoretical significance, compare results across experiments or studies, or conduct meta-analyses. This is particularly important because the reported raw B values for go-past time (~41–43 ms) and regressions-out (~0.25–0.30 log-odds) are difficult to contextualize without standardization.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001) such that go-past times were longer for incongruent trials than for congruent ones.

issues.description: No a priori power analyses are reported for any of the three experiments. The sample sizes (N = 46, 29, and 47) are modest and asymmetric across experiments. Experiment 2 with N = 29 is particularly underpowered for detecting suffix-level interaction effects involving 11 suffixes and graded specificity. Given the use of generalized mixed models with crossed random effects, power depends on both participant and item counts; the item counts are also low (80, 66, and 120 trials respectively).
issues.quote: Participants were 29 undergraduate students from Royal Holloway University of London. Sampling conditions were otherwise the same as in Experiment 1.

issues.description: In Experiment 2, suffix spellings were 'manually extracted from whole nonword spellings' to create the binary dependent variable. No inter-rater reliability statistic (e.g., Cohen's κ) is reported, nor is it stated whether a second rater verified the extraction. Given that participants could produce non-standard or ambiguous spellings of nonword endings (e.g., partial spellings, creative segmentations), the coding decisions could be systematically biased in a way that inflates the congruency effect.
issues.quote: Suffix spellings were manually extracted from whole nonword spellings (1,914 analysable data points). The dependent variable was binary and coded whether the actual spelling was the target spelling for this suffix or not

issues.description: Experiment 1 had 11.7% missing data due to timeouts and button-press errors. No information is provided about how these trials were handled in the analysis (excluded as missing, coded as errors, imputed). Critically, missing data arising from a 2-second timeout are not random: they are more likely for harder, more ambiguous items. Systematic exclusion of difficult trials would bias the estimated sensitivity to diagnosticity upward, inflating the main finding.
issues.quote: We used generalised mixed modelling analysis from the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2014) on 1,625 data points (11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response).

issues.description: Beyond the absent item random intercept, the model for Experiment 1 also contains no random slopes. Given that condition varies within subjects (participants see both adjective- and noun-diagnostic items), the by-subject random effect of condition is not modeled. Maximal random effects structures are recommended for crossed designs to avoid inflated Type I error rates. The minimal (intercept-only) structure used is likely anti-conservative.
issues.quote: This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.description: The General Discussion concludes that 'diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.' This universal claim is unsupported by any data from other writing systems, and the authors acknowledge that 'further research is needed.' The hedged qualifier 'in one way or another' is too vague to constitute a falsifiable prediction. Making a universalist claim in the Discussion without empirical support from other orthographies is an overclaim.
issues.quote: It is our view that diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.

issues.description: To combine noun- and adjective-diagnostic suffixes in a single regression, the authors multiply diagnosticity by −1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes. This transformation is described briefly but its justification and its effects on the interpretation of the resulting estimate are not fully examined. The decision is made after observing that a condition-based analysis was significant, and the transformation is validated only by separate sub-analyses. Performing the transformation and then checking it post-hoc introduces researcher degrees of freedom not acknowledged in the paper.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable.

issues.description: In the regressions-out section of Experiment 3, three separate B values and z values are reported for apparently related contrasts without a clear table or summary distinguishing them: B = 0.3 / z = 3.12 (main congruency effect), B = -0.15 / z = -2.31 (diagnosticity in congruent condition), B = 0.21 / z = 1.8 (diagnosticity in incongruent condition), and B = 0.37 / z = 3.744 (interaction). The relationship among these estimates is inconsistent with a standard interaction parameterization: the interaction term (0.37) should approximately equal the difference in simple slopes (0.21 − (−0.15) = 0.36), which is borderline consistent, but the main effect reported in the text (B = 0.3 for congruency) does not appear in Table 5, which shows B = 0.25. These inconsistencies suggest the estimates come from non-identical models.
issues.quote: there was a main effect of diagnosticity: the probability of regressing to previous regions of the sentence decreased as diagnosticity increased in the congruent condition (B = -0.15, z = -2.31, p < 0.05), and increased as diagnosticity increased in the incongruent condition (marginal significance, B = 0.21, z = 1.8, p = 0.08). Second, there was an interaction between diagnosticity and congruency such that the probability of regression became higher as diagnosticity increased in the incongruent condition (B = 0.37, z = 3.744, p < 0.001)

issues.description: The paper interprets a regression slope of 0.9 from the model lm(Hspelling ~ Hphonology) as evidence that 'the spellings of derivational suffixes generally yield better prediction of lexical category than do their spoken realisations.' However, this interpretation is only valid if the intercept is zero or negligible. A slope < 1 combined with a positive intercept would mean that for high-entropy phonological forms, spelling is more predictable, but for low-entropy forms, spelling could be less predictable. The intercept is not reported, making the stated conclusion potentially misleading. Moreover, the comparison of 'mean H' values (Hspelling = 0.61 vs Hsound = 0.63) is a paired comparison that should be tested directly rather than inferred from a regression slope.
issues.quote: A slope less than 1 would support our conjecture that spelling is more predictive of category compared to phonology. We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 (SE = 0.04, t = 25.32, p < 0.0001), and that this slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01). That is, the spellings of derivational suffixes generally yield better prediction of lexical category (mean H=0.61) than do their spoken realisations (mean H=0.63).
